headline: LLM APIs pass all 20 coding tasks, but speed varies 10x across providers
summary: A benchmark of free and paid LLM APIs for coding shows 100% success on real-world tasks, but response times can differ by up to 23x between providers. The free tier landscape has shifted significantly in the past year.
details: A recent benchmark tested four LLM API providers (three free, one paid) on five real coding tasks. All 20 runs passed on the first attempt, demonstrating high correctness across providers.
The primary difference observed was speed, with response times varying by up to 23x. This highlights that while LLMs are highly capable for coding, performance efficiency is a key differentiator.

The free tier landscape for LLM APIs has drastically changed in the last 12 months. Many previously recommended free options now require payment or have been deprecated, making current benchmarks essential for developers.

The testing methodology involved running each task in a fresh git worktree, parsing model responses, writing new files, and verifying results with existing test suites. No human edits or retries were allowed.

For a multi-file change task, OpenRouter completed it in just 2.7 seconds, while another provider took 61.7 seconds. This significant speed difference impacts the user experience for interactive coding agents.

For personal coding work, OpenRouter emerged as a surprise winner due to its speed. For team-based workflows, the Cline API, a single-billed aggregator for Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, offers a clean and competitively priced paid solution.

headline_marked: [[Trump Administration Sides With OpenAI]] in NYT Copyright Lawsuit over LLM training
headline: Trump Administration Sides With OpenAI in NYT Copyright Lawsuit over LLM training
summary: The US government has filed a letter supporting OpenAI in its legal battle with The New York Times, arguing on the issue of training large language models on copyrighted material.
details: The Trump Administration has formally taken OpenAI's side in the ongoing copyright infringement lawsuit filed by The New York Times. This intervention comes in the form of a letter to the US district judge overseeing the case.

While the letter specifically addresses the New York Times and OpenAI dispute, the government clarified that its arguments are intended to apply broadly to all parties involved in this and related cases, including other publishers and authors.

Intellectual property lawyer Evan Brown noted that while the presiding judge, Sidney H. Stein, is not legally bound by the letter, it will likely be taken "quite seriously." This is due to its origin from the Department of Justice, which inherently carries significant weight in legal proceedings.
Neither OpenAI nor Microsoft, a key partner, immediately provided a comment when approached by WIRED regarding the administration's stance.
